claims.claim: Rab27, Rab32, Rab23, and Rab9 are more likely to serve cell-specific functions.
claims.source: By contrast, Rab27, Rab32, Rab23, and Rab9 are more likely to serve cell-specific functions, consistent with previous observations for each of the four in Drosophila (Chan et al., 2011; Dong et al., 2013; Gillingham et al., 2014; Lien et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion of the study and supported by citations to Chan et al., 2011; Dong et al., 2013; Gillingham et al., 2014; Lien et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2004.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on Rab GTPases, including their discovery, function, and evolutionary conservation across species. Rab GTPases were initially discovered in brain tissue, function as key regulators of membrane trafficking, and are highly conserved between Drosophila and humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These claims establish the scientific context and are consistent with established knowledge in the field. The evolutionary conservation data (C8) is particularly well-supported.

results.result: The manuscript cites prior work linking specific Rab GTPases to neurological diseases and synaptic function, including rab7 mutations causing CMT2B neuropathy, Rab10 as a target of LRRK2 in Parkinson's disease, and Rab26/Rab35 involvement in synaptic vesicle recycling.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These claims establish the neurological relevance of Rab GTPases and provide motivation for the current study.

results.result: The authors previously found that all 26 Drosophila Rab GTPases are expressed in the nervous system, with half enriched or strongly enriched in neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 are supported by citations to the authors' prior work (Chan et al., 2011; Jin et al., 2012). This establishes the foundation for the current study's focus on nervous system-enriched Rabs.

results.result: The authors generated a complete collection of rab null mutants using two methods: six mutants via homologous recombination (Gal4 knock-ins) and eleven mutants via CRISPR/Cas9.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C21 describe the methods used to generate the mutant collection. The methods are clearly described and validated by PCR and sequencing as detailed in Materials and Methods. This represents a major technical achievement.

results.result: Of the 26 rab null mutants, seven are homozygous lethal (rab1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 11), one (rab35) is semi-lethal with few male escapers, and 18 are viable as homozygous adults under laboratory conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 present the viability classification of all 26 mutants. The data are clearly presented in Figure 1A and represent a fundamental characterization of the mutant collection. The classification is straightforward and well-documented.

results.result: After 10 generations, only 10 of 18 viable lines lost their balancer chromosomes, indicating that eight rab mutant chromosomes confer a competitive disadvantage.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C26 describe a competitive fitness assay. The observation (C25) is clearly stated and shown in Figure 1B. The inference (C26) is reasonable based on the persistence of balanced flies, though alternative explanations (e.g., linked deleterious mutations) are not explicitly ruled out.

results.result: Two viable rab mutants exhibit fertility defects: rab10 mutants cannot lay eggs, and rab30 mutant males are sterile, producing only non-developing eggs. The rab30 phenotype was rescued by Rab30 overexpression.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 describe fertility phenotypes. The observations (C27-C29) are clearly stated. The rescue experiment (C30) provides genetic validation of the rab30 phenotype, though details of the rescue are limited to a reference to Materials and Methods.

results.result: All lethal rab mutants are in ubiquitously expressed genes, while all 13 nervous system-enriched Rab GTPases are viable and fertile under laboratory conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 present a striking correlation between expression pattern and viability. This is clearly shown in Figure 1A and represents a major finding of the study. The binary categorization is remarkable and well-documented.

results.result: All 13 nervous system-enriched Rabs are expressed in different patterns in both the developing and adult brain, as revealed by endogenous expression patterns from available knock-ins.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 describe expression patterns shown in supplementary figures. The data are based on prior work (Dunst et al., 2015) and provide important context for functional analyses. The patterns are well-documented in Figure 1—figure supplements 2-3.

results.result: Of 16 homozygous viable and fertile mutants, 12 exhibited developmental timing defects, two showed wing development defects, and only rab21 and rab26 showed no developmental defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 summarize the developmental phenotyping results. The data are clearly presented and represent a comprehensive characterization. The statement that only rab21 and rab26 showed no defects is notable and well-supported.

results.result: rabX4 exhibited the longest overall developmental delay at all three temperatures, with most eggs failing to develop and only few adult escapers showing 2-4 day delays.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 describe the most severe developmental phenotype. The data are shown in Figure 2 and supplementary files. The phenotype is clearly documented and represents an extreme case among viable mutants.

results.result: rabX1 was the only mutant with selective embryo development delays at all temperatures but normal larval and pupal timing. rabX1 flies laid very few eggs with only 20% developing to adulthood.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 describe a stage-specific developmental phenotype. The data are shown in Figure 2D-L and Supplementary file 4. The specificity of the embryonic delay is notable and well-documented.

results.result: rab19 was the only mutant with selective pupal development delays at all temperatures. Additionally, rab19 showed 50-80% late pupal lethality specifically at 29°C, with all surviving adults dying within days.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 describe temperature-sensitive lethality. The data are shown in Figure 2D-L. The temperature-specific lethality is striking and suggests a critical role for rab19 at elevated temperatures.

results.result: rab32 exhibited increased late pupal lethality specifically at 29°C, while at 18°C it showed mild overall developmental delay due to delayed larval development.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 describe temperature-dependent phenotypes. The data are shown in Figure 2A,G. The temperature-specific effects are well-documented.

results.result: Several mutants (rab40, rabX6, rab39, rab3, rab4) exhibited mild developmental delays specifically at 18°C, with phenotypes validated in alternate genetic backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 describe cold-sensitive developmental phenotypes. The validation in alternate genetic backgrounds (backcrossed or over deficiencies) strengthens these findings. The data are shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

results.result: rab9 and rab14 showed shorter larval development at 18°C (validated over deficiencies), while rab18 showed shortened pupal development specifically at 29°C (validated in backcrossed background).
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 describe accelerated development phenotypes. These are notable as most other mutants show delays. The validation strengthens these findings. Data are shown in Figure 2G,L and supplementary figures.

results.result: Temperature affects wing size in control flies (25-45% larger at 18°C vs 29°C). At 18°C, rab3, rab19, and rab27 had smaller wings while rabX1 and rabX4 had larger wings. At 29°C, rabX6 had smaller wings and rab9 had larger wings.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 describe wing size phenotypes. The control observation (C53) establishes the temperature effect. The mutant phenotypes are shown in Figure 2M,N and validated in alternate backgrounds (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The correlation between developmental delay and wing size for rabX1/rabX4 is notable.

results.result: The rab23 null mutant exhibited a previously reported planar cell polarity phenotype of wing bristles, plus a newly observed highly penetrant p-cv vein shortening (90% at 18°C, ameliorated to 12% at 29°C).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 describe wing phenotypes. The PCP phenotype (C58) is supported by prior citations. The vein shortening phenotype (C59) is newly reported and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3. The temperature-dependence is striking.

results.result: In summary, 14 of 16 viable and fertile null mutants exhibit specific developmental defects, most of which only occurred or were exacerbated at extreme temperatures (18°C or 29°C).
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 summarize the developmental phenotyping. The summary is well-supported by the detailed data presented in Figure 2 and supplementary materials. The temperature-dependence is a major finding.

results.result: In control flies, continuous light stimulation leads to gradual decline of ERG 'on' transient amplitude and depolarization over 7 days. Two days of light stimulation represents a sensitized period with dynamic range for detecting defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 describe the establishment of a functional assay. The sensitization curves are shown in Figure 3A-B. The identification of 2 days as an optimal timepoint is well-justified and provides a rational basis for subsequent experiments.

results.result: None of the mutants exhibited significant reductions in ERG 'on' transient or depolarization immediately after hatching (0 day).
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 establish that mutants have normal initial function. This is shown in Figure 3C-D and is important for distinguishing developmental from functional maintenance defects.

results.result: After 2 days of light stimulation, six rab mutants (rab3, rab14, rab19, rab26, rab30, rabX6) showed reduced neurotransmission. Five of these (rab3, rab19, rab26, rab30, rabX6) had specific synaptic defects without depolarization changes, while rab14 showed both reduced transmission and depolarization.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 describe stimulus-dependent functional defects. The data are clearly presented and the distinction between synaptic-specific and general cellular defects is important. The correlation with nervous system-enriched expression is notable.

results.result: The five rabs with specific synaptic defects (rab3, rab19, rab26, rab30, rabX6) showed no defects without light stimulus, while rab14 and rab27 showed reduced transmission and depolarization after 4 days in the dark.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 distinguish stimulus-dependent from aging-dependent defects. The dark-rearing control is critical for this interpretation. The data are clearly presented in Figure 3G-H.

results.result: The synaptic defects of rab3, rab19, rab26, rab30, and rabX6 are stimulus-dependent, while the defects of rab14 and rab27 are aging-dependent functional maintenance defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 present interpretations of the functional data. The inference is reasonable based on the differential effects of light stimulation vs. dark rearing. However, the distinction between 'stimulus-dependent' and 'aging-dependent' could be more nuanced, as both involve time.

results.result: None of the 18 viable rab mutants exhibited elevated levels of the apoptotic marker DCP-1 before or after 2 days of light stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C74 rules out apoptosis as a mechanism for functional defects. This is shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The negative result is important for interpreting the functional defects.

results.result: No rhabdomere defects were found in any viable mutants before stimulation, but after 2 days of light stimulation, rhabdomere structures exhibited highly increased variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 describe structural changes in photoreceptors. The data are shown in Figure 4A,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The stimulus-dependent structural changes are consistent with the functional defects.

results.result: In control, rhabdomere area increased ~30% after 2 days of stimulation, while seven rab mutants (rab4, rab18, rab21, rab27, rab30, rab32, rab40) showed significant area decreases.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 describe quantitative changes in rhabdomere area. The data are shown in Figure 4D. The control increase is notable and the mutant decreases suggest defects in membrane turnover.

results.result: Rhabdomere shapes showed increased variability and significant changes in three additional rab mutants (rab19, rab23, rab26) after 2 days of light stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 describes shape changes distinct from area changes. The data are shown in Figure 4E-F. The shape analysis provides additional information about membrane organization.

results.result: At least 10 of the 18 viable rab mutants affect membrane turnover in rhabdomeres when challenged with continuous stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is a conclusion based on the rhabdomere area and shape data. The conclusion is well-supported by the quantitative data presented in Figure 4D-F.

results.result: All 13 nervous system-enriched rab mutants had normal axonal projections in newly hatched flies, except rabX1 which showed unusual Chaoptin accumulations in non-photoreceptor cell bodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 describe axon morphology. The data are shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5A. The rabX1 phenotype is consistent with prior observations in endomembrane degradation mutants.

results.result: After 2 days of light stimulation, rab26 and to a lesser extent rab19 mutants exhibited distinct membrane accumulations at the distal tips of R1-R6 photoreceptor axon terminals.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 describes stimulus-dependent morphological changes. The data are shown in Figure 5A. This phenotype is consistent with the functional defects observed in these mutants.

results.result: None of the five neuronal rab mutants with synaptic maintenance defects showed altered Atg8 labeling. In contrast, rabX1 showed increased Atg8 in cell bodies prior to stimulation, and rab23, rab27, rab32, and rabX1 showed stimulus-dependent increases in Atg8-positive compartments in axon terminals.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 examine autophagy markers. The data are shown in Figure 5B. The lack of Atg8 changes in mutants with synaptic defects suggests autophagy-independent mechanisms.

results.result: In wild type, Rab11 is strongly upregulated in synaptic terminals after 2 days of light stimulation. The same stimulus-dependent increase was found in all mutants except rabX1.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 examine recycling endosome markers. The data are shown in Figure 5C. The normal Rab11 upregulation in most mutants suggests that canonical recycling pathways are intact.

results.result: rab26 is one of the mutants with reduced stimulus-dependent functional maintenance and one of only two mutants without developmental defects. rab26 null mutant axon terminals showed pronounced membrane accumulations after light stimulation, but no significant changes in Atg8/LC3.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 focus on rab26 as a case study. The data are shown in Figures 2, 3E, 5A-B. The lack of Atg8 changes challenges the prior hypothesis linking Rab26 to autophagy.

results.result: Expression of GTP-locked Rab26 in adult photoreceptor neurons led to complete loss of neurotransmission, while neither complete loss of rab26 function nor expression of GDP-locked Rab26 significantly affected neurotransmission in newly hatched flies.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 describe dominant effects of GTP-locked Rab26. The data are shown in Figure 6A. The severe effect of GTP-locked Rab26 contrasts with the mild effect of the null mutant, suggesting that constitutive activation is more disruptive than loss of function.

results.result: Compartments marked by YFP-tagged WT or GTP-locked Rab26 largely exclude synaptic markers (Syt1, CSP) and autophagosome marker Atg8, but show elevated levels of recycling endosomal marker Rab11 and endosomal markers Hrs and Syx7.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 describe Rab26 localization. The data are shown in Figure 6B-G. The exclusion from synaptic vesicle and autophagosome markers, combined with colocalization with endosomal markers, suggests an endosomal rather than synaptic vesicle or autophagy role.

results.result: Adult brains mutant for rab26 did not exhibit obvious changes of Atg8 or Syt1 and appeared morphologically normal with no differences in any markers analyzed.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 describe the null mutant phenotype. The data are shown in Figure 6H-K. The lack of obvious defects in the null mutant contrasts with the severe effects of GTP-locked Rab26 overexpression.

results.result: At the NMJ, Rab26 is present at presynaptic boutons but not postsynaptic muscle. Rab26 partially colocalizes with Rab11, CSP, Syt1, and Syx7, but none of these markers were affected in the rab26 null mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 describe Rab26 localization at the NMJ. The data are shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B. The lack of marker changes in the null mutant is consistent with the brain observations.

results.result: Overexpressed YFP-tagged Rab26 variants (WT, GDP-locked, GTP-locked) showed varying colocalization with synaptic vesicle and endosomal markers at the NMJ, but no obvious disruption of their localization or levels. No effect on Atg8 was found.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105 describe overexpression effects at the NMJ. The data are shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-F. The lack of Atg8 effects is consistent with other observations.

results.result: In the adult brain, Rab26 immunolabeling revealed synaptic neuropils at varying levels in different regions and colocalized well with endogenously tagged Rab26. In the lamina, Rab26 showed a punctate pattern across photoreceptor axon terminals and a row of cells distal of the lamina.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 describe Rab26 distribution in the adult brain. The data are shown in Figure 6M,O,P. The validation with endogenously tagged Rab26 strengthens the antibody specificity.

results.result: Co-labeling with glia marker ebony showed a largely complementary pattern to Rab26 in the lamina. The synaptic marker Brp revealed a small subset of colocalizing synapses selectively in the proximal regions of axon terminals, where continuous stimulation led to protein accumulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110 describe cell-type specificity and synaptic localization. The data are shown in Figure 6P. The correlation between Brp colocalization and the site of protein accumulations is notable.

results.result: Mutant accumulations of Chaoptin became more pronounced with 4 days of light stimulation in rab26 mutants. This phenotype was mimicked by photoreceptor-specific Rab26 RNAi and rescued by photoreceptor-specific Rab26 expression, indicating a cell-autonomous phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C114 describe the rab26 phenotype and its validation. The data are shown in Figure 7A-D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-E. The RNAi and rescue experiments provide strong genetic evidence for cell autonomy.

results.result: The protein accumulations in rab26 mutants after 4 days of light stimulation were specifically enriched for Chaoptin and N-Cadherin (CadN), but not Atg8, Syt1, Rab5, or Rab7. Of endosomal markers, only Syx7 was significantly increased.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 characterize the protein accumulations. The data are shown in Figure 7E-M. The selective enrichment of transmembrane receptors (Chaoptin, CadN) and exclusion of synaptic vesicle and autophagy markers is important for understanding the mechanism.

results.result: Continuous stimulation leads to the selective accumulation of presynaptic transmembrane receptors, including Chaoptin and CadN, specifically in the most proximal part of photoreceptor terminals in rab26 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 is a conclusion based on the protein accumulation data. The conclusion is well-supported by the data in Figure 7E-M.

results.result: L4 neurons specifically form synapses at the most proximal end of photoreceptor axon terminals, function in progressive motion detection, and are cholinergic based on expression of vesicular acetylcholine transporter and ChAT.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 provide context from prior work about L4 neurons. These claims are supported by appropriate citations and establish the anatomical and functional context for interpreting the rab26 phenotype.

results.result: Immunolabeling of presynaptic ChAT and postsynaptic cholinergic receptor Dα7 revealed increased levels of both proteins after 4 days of light stimulation in rab26 mutants, with ChAT increases specific to the proximal lamina and Dα7 across the entire lamina.
results.evaluation: Claim C122 describes changes in cholinergic markers. The data are shown in Figure 7N-Q. The spatial specificity of ChAT increases is consistent with the localization of protein accumulations.

results.result: Across the optic lobe, the endogenous Rab26 knock-in exhibits an expression pattern similar to ChAT.
results.evaluation: Claim C123 describes Rab26 expression pattern. The data are shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F. The similarity to ChAT expression is consistent with a role in cholinergic circuits.

results.result: Photoreceptors that terminate in the lamina are not known to be cholinergic, and they neither express ChAT nor the Dα7 receptor based on a recent systematic transcriptome analysis.
results.evaluation: Claim C124 is supported by citation to Davis et al., 2020. This establishes that photoreceptors are not the source of cholinergic signaling.

results.result: L4 and lamina wide-field feedback (Lawf) neurons are both cholinergic and provide synaptic input to R1-R6 photoreceptor axon terminals.
results.evaluation: Claim C125 is supported by citations to Davis et al., 2020 and Rivera-Alba et al., 2011. This establishes the circuit context for cholinergic input to photoreceptors.

results.result: Co-labeling of L4 and Lawf neurons with Rab26 and ChAT revealed that the Rab26-positive cells distal of the lamina were Lawf2 neurons, while ChAT-positive labeling in the proximal lamina colocalized with L4. Rab26 labeling was complementary to ChAT-positive L4 collaterals.
results.evaluation: Claim C126 describes cell-type identification. The data are shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G-I. This establishes that Rab26 is expressed in Lawf2 neurons but not L4 neurons.

results.result: Photoreceptors are predicted to express a single acetylcholine receptor subunit, Dα4.
results.evaluation: Claim C127 is supported by citations to Rivera-Alba et al., 2011 and Davis et al., 2020. This establishes that photoreceptors can receive cholinergic input.

results.result: Dα4 RNAi exhibited no obvious defects prior to stimulation, but after 4 days of light stimulation, photoreceptor-specific Dα4 RNAi led to both Rab26-positive accumulations in the lamina and proximal Chaoptin accumulations characteristic of the rab26 mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129 describe the effect of reducing cholinergic input. The data are shown in Figure 7R and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The phenocopy of the rab26 mutant is striking and suggests a functional link.

results.result: Loss of rab26 in photoreceptors has a stimulus-dependent effect similar to decreased cholinergic input onto photoreceptor axon terminals, which function as postsynaptic partners.
results.evaluation: Claim C130 is an interpretation based on the Dα4 RNAi experiments. The inference is reasonable but the mechanism linking Rab26 to cholinergic signaling remains unclear. Further experiments would be needed to establish a direct mechanistic link.

results.result: All previously described nervous system-enriched Rab GTPases are viable under laboratory conditions. However, challenging development with temperature or function with continuous stimulation revealed distinct requirements for all homozygous viable rabs. The findings suggest that the majority of Rab GTPases modulate membrane trafficking to maintain robust development and function under challenging environmental conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C133 present the main conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the comprehensive phenotyping data presented throughout the manuscript. The conclusion that Rabs provide robustness under challenging conditions is a major conceptual advance.

results.result: Viability vs lethality is not a binary distinction of the null mutants, but represents a continuous range of context-dependent phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claim C134 is a conceptual conclusion supported by the data showing temperature-dependent lethality, competitive disadvantages, and stimulus-dependent defects. The citation to Hiesinger, 2021 provides additional context.

results.result: All mutants with stimulus-dependent functional maintenance defects exhibit strong adult synaptic localization. The majority of Rabs with adult synaptic localization (Rab3, Rab26, Rab19, RabX6, Rab30, RabX4) serve modulatory functions that become apparent under challenging conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C136 correlate localization with function. The data are shown in Table 1. The correlation is notable and supports the idea that synaptic Rabs provide functional robustness.

results.result: Rab27, Rab32, Rab23, and Rab9 are more likely to serve cell-specific functions, consistent with previous observations in Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claim C137 is supported by the data and citations to prior work. The distinction between modulatory and cell-specific functions is reasonable based on the phenotypic data.
